title: Anger: Wisdom for Cooling the Flames
source_note: Full text not readable (archive PDF returned font-encoded stream; Wikipedia pages 404). Facts come from verbatim quote pages and search summaries of the book's text. Thin sourcing.

facts.claim: Anger is compared to a potato: a raw potato cannot be eaten; mindfulness is the fire that cooks the potatoes of anger.
facts.source: search summary of book text (archive PDF), library review quoting him

facts.claim: Verbatim quote: 'Anger is like a howling baby, suffering and crying. The baby needs his mother to embrace him.'
A passage pictures a mother who strikes her crying baby and fails to see that she and the child are one; we are the mothers of our own anger.

Mindful breathing gives the caring energy of a mother; simply embracing anger and breathing in and out is enough. Verbatim: 'When anger comes up in us, we should begin to practice mindful breathing right away'.
Verbatim: 'we should try not to do anything or say anything when we are angry.'
Verbatim: 'You discover that the main cause of your suffering is the seed of anger in you, because it has been watered too often, by yourself and by other people.'
Verbatim: 'You have to protect yourself and your beloved ones by practicing selective watering.'
Anger is likened to garbage that can become compost, and compost becomes a flower (reader note and review); 'cooling the flames' is in the subtitle.
Anger is read as a sign that something needs taking care of; one can care for it like a crying baby (pick up, speak quietly, find what is wrong).
Thich Nhat Hanh is a Vietnamese monk.
